```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(4321)

# Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)
library(showtext)

# Fonts ------------------------------------------------------------------------
font_add_google("Bangers")

showtext_auto(enable = TRUE)
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)

# Theme ------------------------------------------------------------------------
theme_pres <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Bangers", base_size = 16) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(size = rel(1), face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = rel(1))
    )
}

# The data ---------------------------------------------------------------------
hero_data <- tibble::tibble(
  hours_trained = rnorm(10, mean = 7, sd = 2),
  villains_defeated = 10 + 2 * hours_trained + rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 2)
)

# Reconstructing the crime scene
fit <- glm(villains_defeated ~ hours_trained, data = hero_data)

hero_data <- hero_data |> dplyr::mutate(preds = predict(fit))
```

# Issue 01: The Markov Files {.section}

## The Markov Files {.panel}

The world is always changing.

- The weather shifts
- Markets rise and fall
- Health fades and recovers.

At first glance, it looks like chaos.

But hidden inside that chaos...

are patterns.

::: {.caption .fragment}
Patterns we can model
:::

## The Hero {.panel}

::: {layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="center"}

::: {.fragment}
![](files/images/markov_man.png)
:::

::: {.speech .fragment}
I protect the system...
one transition at a time.
:::
:::

::: {.caption .fragment}
His superpower lies in one simple rule ...
:::

## The Superpower {.panel}

::: {.incremental}
- Systems move between a finite number of states.
- Let $X_t$ represent the state at time $t$.
- Each state belongs to $S = \{1, 2, \dots, K\}$.
- **The next state depends only on the current state.**
:::

<br>

::: {.fragment .fade-up .callout-important title="Markov Man's Superpower"}
$$
P(X_{t+1} = j \; \vert \; X_t = i, X_{t-1} = i_{t-1}, \dots X_0 = i_0) = P(X_{t+1} = j \; \vert \; X_t = i)
$$

:::

::: {.caption .fragment}
No history. No memory. Only the present.
:::

## {.explosion}

BUT WAIT!

{{< bam "A WEAKNESS!" colour=red top=28% right=12% rotate=10 size=1.5em fragment=burst index=1 >}}

# Issue 02: Markov Man's Hidden Weakness {.section}

## The Clues {.panel}

In regression, the suspect leaves behind a trail.

::: {.incremental}
- **A fitted value**
- **A residual**
- **A clue**
:::

## Scene 1: The Evidence {.panel}

```{r}
#| label: fig-1
#| fig-cap: "Raw evidence collected from the scene."

hero_data |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_trained, villains_defeated)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours of training",
    y = "Villains defeated"
  ) +
  theme_pres()
```

## Scene 2: The Suspects {.panel}

```{r}
#| label: fig-2
#| fig-cap: "The prime suspect enters the frame."

hero_data |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_trained, villains_defeated)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_smooth(
    formula = y ~ x,
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(5)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours of training",
    y = "Villains defeated"
  ) +
  theme_pres()
```

## Scene 3: The Reconstruction {.panel}

```{r}
#| label: fig-3
#| fig-cap: "The suspect gives their version of events"

hero_data |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_trained, villains_defeated)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_smooth(
    formula = y ~ x,
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(5)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = preds),
    size = 3.5,
    colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(3)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours of training",
    y = "Villains defeated"
  ) +
  theme_pres()
```

## Scene 4: The Clues {.panel}

```{r}
#| label: fig-4
#| fig-cap: "The inconsistencies begin to show"

hero_data |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_trained, villains_defeated)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_smooth(
    formula = y ~ x,
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(5)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = preds),
    size = 3.5,
    colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(3)
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = hours_trained,
      xend = hours_trained,
      y = villains_defeated,
      yend = preds
    ),
    linewidth = 1.2,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours of training",
    y = "Villains defeated"
  ) +
  theme_pres()
```

## {.explosion}

BUT WAIT!

{{< bam "PLOT TWIST!" colour=yellow top=10% right=10% rotate=8 size=2.8em fragment=burst index=1 >}}
{{< bam "NO RESIDUALS?!" colour=red bottom=18% left=15% rotate=-6 size=2.2em fragment=pop index=2 >}}

## Markov Man hits a dead end {.panel}

But Markov models **leave no such trail**.

::: {.callout-note title="They predict probabilities"}
$$
P = \begin{bmatrix}
P(A \rightarrow A) \quad P(A \rightarrow B) \\
P(B \rightarrow A) \quad P(B \rightarrow B)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 \quad 0.4 \\
0.7 \quad 0.3
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.thought .fragment}
How do you compute residuals from probabilities?
:::

## The Alibi Check {.panel}

```{r}
#| label: fig-5
#| fig-cap: "The transition matrix"
transitions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~From , ~To , ~Observed , ~Predicted ,
  "A"   , "A" , 0.83      , 0.60       ,
  "A"   , "B" , 0.17      , 0.40       ,
  "B"   , "A" , 0.33      , 0.70       ,
  "B"   , "B" , 0.66      , 0.30
)

transitions |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Observed:Predicted),
    names_to = "transition",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = To, y = From, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(value * 100, "%")), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "OrYel") +
  facet_wrap(
    ~transition,
    labeller = labeller(
      transition = c(
        "Observed" = "Witness Testimony",
        "Predicted" = "Suspect Alibi"
      )
    )
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_pres() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

::: {.caption .fragment}
Do the stories match?
:::

## Markov Man {.speech}

If residuals fail us...

we need to find another way.

# Issue 03: Markov Man's Investigation {.section}

To solve the mystery...

Markov Man ran thousands of simulated investigations.

... specifically 54,000!

## The Reconstruction {.panel}

::: {.incremental}
- $10{,}000$ individuals investigated
- $3 \rightarrow 5$ waves observed
- $5$ covariates generated
- $3 \rightarrow 5$ states examined
- $3$ **suspects** tested
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up .callout-tip title="The Suspects"}

**Base model**: $y \sim x_1 + x_2 + x_3$

**Additive model**: $y \sim x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + y_{t-1}$

**Multiplicative Model**: $y \sim (x_1 + x_2 + x_3) \times y_{t-1}$

:::

## Evidence Processing {.panel}

For every fitted model:

:::{.incremental}
- First, Markov Man record what actually happened: $P$
- Next, Markov Man reconstruct what the model expected: $\hat{P}$
- Finally, Markov Man compare the two stories: $P \longleftrightarrow \hat{P}$
:::

<br>

::: {.fragment .fade-up .narration}
The greater the difference, the greater the suspicion.
:::

## Detective Gadgets {.panel}

Markov Man assembled his specialist detective squad:

::: {layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="center"}
::: {.fragment}
- Frobenius Norm
- Manhattan Distance
- Maximum Absolute Error
- Root Mean Squared
- Correlation Dissimilarity
- Kullback-Leibler divergence
:::

::: {.fragment}
As well as some of his most **trusted veterans**

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="The Veteran Detectives"}
**AIC and BIC**
:::
:::
:::

## Case closed {.panel}

The investigation revealed:

::: {.incremental}
- For smaller sample sizes, **Manhattan Distance** and **Mean Absolute
  Difference** were the strongest detectives.
- In some cases, they **outperformed** the veteran detectives.
- However, when there was a **great number of states**, the detectives were
  **all confused**.
:::

::: {.narration .fragment}
For small samples, we have a couple of good detectives!
:::

## Press release {.speech}

"When sample sizes are small and states are few, Manhattan Distance is your
best detective!"
